carried.lens: the grader and the measurement itself: extraction, equivalence, seeds, set composition, what a count hides
carried.statement: A count 'at 16,384' rescored from a 32k run is a different measurement from a native 16k run: rows longer than 16,384 count wrong, while a native run lets grader v3 credit a box already written inside a truncated row (RL 69 % of capped rows, base 17 %, Think-SFT rarely). So 32k-minus-16k is extension finishes only, and models that box mid-reasoning lose a few problems when rescored.

carried.lens: weight space: the RL weight change, its top directions, scaling and transplanting it
carried.statement: Within the top-8 RL directions, the first singular direction of each matrix carries the format and stop part: it cuts cap hits, and at large size stops the model boxing its answer. Directions 2-8 carry the part that raises right answers on finished problems. So rank-1 edits finish without adding right answers, removing direction 1 keeps most of the correctness gain, and overdosing direction 1 produces unboxed answers that are graded wrong.

holds_against.why: One direction already gives 181 of top-8's 192, but it does so by finishing (cap hits 77 -> 51) at the base's precision; k=8 and k=64 add right answers on finished problems.
Top-1 at 2x reaches 184, as many as 8 directions in layers 0-10, but it gets there by converting cap hits (23 left) at lower precision, and at 3x it falls to 168 with 67 unboxed answers.

carried.lens: the grader and the measurement itself: extraction, equivalence, seeds, set composition, what a count hides
carried.statement: A count's size depends on the set's difficulty mix: hard328's first 164 problems are much harder than its second half (cued base 65 vs 99), and fresh2026 is harder still. On hard items the opening (cue, step 100, self-opening) moves few problems, while answers past 16k tokens are mostly unfinished or guessed, so cap raises and votes yield less per abstention than on hard328, and plain prompts keep a falling share of the cued count.

holds_against.why: The cue keeps 77 % of RL's gain on MMLU-Pro/BBH as on MATH-500, but those are short-answer sets with no cap pressure; the claim is about long hard sets.
Plain/cue is 0.55 on MATH-500 and 0.46 on hard328; 76 sits on that falling line, which predicts ~0.44 on fresh2026.

carried.lens: training data and objective: what Think-SFT imitation, RL reward and pretraining each put into the model, exposure of problems
carried.statement: Think-SFT imitated teacher traces inside its ChatML template, opened by <think> and closed by a final answer after the thinking block. Where and how it states the answer is learned conditional on that template. On the raw template with the cue it reasons as well but sometimes misplaces the final answer (on the line after 'Answer:'), which v3 misses. Its own template restores the trained ending: more MATH-500 answers counted, unchanged reasoning length and cap behaviour on hard328.

holds_against.why: Raw template without the cue is neither the trained template nor the cue's register, so it loses 16; the native template is the trained one.
The misses are about which line carries the answer, not answer type, so the non-integer share need not rise above the pool's.

carried.direct_test: holds (result-ab26c4: Think-SFT's own ChatML <think> template does not make it drift less on hard328 (first 16,384 tokens): drifted share equals raw template + cue within raw-cue seed scatter)

carried.lens: when and how the model stops: token cap, loops, end-of-text, answer markers
carried.statement: On a hard set part of every model's answers would end past 16,384 tokens, and a cut answer scores zero. A change that leaves the length distribution in place (100 RL steps, the cue on a checkpoint, a new seed or more samples) can move only the precision of finished answers. Step 100 writes cued-base lengths at T 1.0 (4,120 vs 4,008 tokens), so on hard problems it keeps the cued base's cap hits and adds a few right answers.

holds_against.why: Step 100's finished answers are 4.6 points more often right than the cued base's. That is a precision gain on finished answers, which the mechanism allows; on the first 164 it is worth about 5 problems.
At T 0.6 step 100 has 103 cap hits against the cued base's 119. At T 0.6, loops that depend on the opening add cap hits; at T 1.0 there are no loops and the lengths match.

carried.direct_test: holds (result-074b77: At T 1.0 on MATH-500, RL step 100 (plain) hits the 16,384-token cap as often as the cued base on the same problems (paired difference not 1 point or more lower), while final RL's cap-hit rate is clearly lower.)

carried.lens: Any family of causes.
carried.statement: A capped sample gives no answer, so in a plurality vote it abstains instead of adding a wrong value. Think-SFT's vote sits near its pass@4 because its unsolved samples run to the cap rather than box a guess. Anything that makes it finish, a 32k cap or the RL difference, turns abstentions into mostly wrong, scattered answers that tie or outvote lone right samples: single scores rise, vote gains shrink.

carried.lens: weight space: the RL weight change, its top directions, scaling and transplanting it
carried.statement: The top RL-Math directions write stop and box logits additively: signed size s shifts the log-odds that an answer runs to the cap by a roughly fixed amount per unit, in either sign, on any set. Cap-hit counts therefore move with each set's base cap rate in log-odds, not by a fixed fraction. Overdose costs right answers only in proportion to a set's long unsolved answers, which it forces to finish as guesses.

holds_against.why: Size 1 has 46 cap hits against 50 at size 0.5, a flat step, but each cell is one sample with an sd of about 6; over sizes -1 to 2 the trend stays monotone (96, 77, 50, 46, 25, 5).
Layers 0-10 alone raise cap hits to 98: a band edit leaves out the late stop readout, and the law covers only the all-layer edit, which drops cap hits to 25.

carried.lens: the grader and the measurement itself: extraction, equivalence, seeds, set composition, what a count hides
carried.statement: Majority vote counts answer strings: the base's wrong answers scatter (only about a quarter repeat), so the right answer is the plurality once per-sample success exceeds about 0.3, and even k leaves ties that a fixed rule breaks about half right. Vote over k therefore rises toward the number of problems whose right answer is the modal string, well below pass@k, with odd k gaining from fewer ties and returns shrinking fast after k = 4.
carried.direct_test: holds (result-dd9b25: On cued-base MATH-500 problems with 2-10 of 12 samples right, the vote over 4 with the real wrong answers beats the same vote with every finished wrong answer merged into one by at least 0.05 per problem.)

carried.lens: training data and objective: what Think-SFT imitation, RL reward and pretraining each put into the model, exposure of problems
carried.statement: Think-SFT copied teacher traces produced under long budgets, and imitation carries no pressure to stop, so its 16,384-token cuts are mid-derivation work, not loops or guesses. More budget turns cut answers right at the problem's difficulty rate (about a quarter on hard328, fewer on 2026 problems). Late finishes are mostly wrong but scattered, so in a vote they seldom beat an existing right answer and add less than to single samples. RL's delta adds stopping, leaving fewer cuts to convert.

holds_against.why: Only the 24 cut answers that switched script before 16k finish right 1 time; the other 69 finish right 22 times, which is the unfinished-work rate the mechanism uses.
The base's late finishes are right 4 of 64 because the base did not imitate long derivations; its cuts are failed solves, the contrast the mechanism expects.

carried.lens: problem structure: difficulty, domain, answer type, length of the needed derivation
carried.statement: An edit's effect splits by problem stratum: it adds right answers on mid-difficulty problems (base right in some samples), which MATH-500 and hard328 both hold in similar numbers, while cap-hit changes live only in the long-derivation tail, which MATH-500 holds about a third as densely. So point gains transfer between sets, but a MATH-500 cap-hit change equals the hard328 change times the base's MATH-500/hard328 cap-hit ratio (about 22.5/77).

holds_against.why: The 1.5x edit gains as much on MATH-500 (+45 of 500) as on hard328 (+36 of 328) in points because the gain is on the mid stratum (23 of 39 gains on already-finished problems), not the tail.
At 2x finished precision falls 0.65 -> 0.59, which looks spread out, but the newly finished answers are the former long cap hits (14 of 77 right), i.e. the tail stratum.

carried.lens: when and how the model stops: token cap, loops, end-of-text, answer markers
carried.statement: A cut-off sample writes no answer marker, so it abstains from the plurality vote instead of voting wrong. A vote's gain over one sample therefore scales with the cap-hit share times the precision of finished answers: Think-SFT (29-46 % capped, 80-88 % precise) votes near pass@4, while RL and the 1.5x edit (5-15 % capped) gain less. A longer cap turns abstentions into mostly wrong late answers, so a vote gains far less from it than one sample does.

holds_against.why: On MATH-500 the base gains +41 under the vote with few cap hits because its wrong finished answers are scattered slips. That is a second source of vote gain that adds to abstention; the ordering across models still follows cap share x precision.
The cued base gains only +8.5 on fresh2026 despite 40 % cap hits because only 36 % of its finished answers are right; abstention pays in proportion to precision, as stated.

carried.lens: weight space: the RL weight change, its top directions, scaling and transplanting it
carried.statement: Edit entries smaller than half a bf16 ulp of the weight they modify are written by stochastic rounding (written/intended cosine 0.585). The written edit is unbiased: the intended direction comes through at full nominal size, and the rounding residue is a random edit, which is inert like the random rank-8 and noise controls. Scores therefore follow the nominal dose. The residue and GPU-dependent rounding draws add sample-to-sample spread, but they do not shift the mean.

holds_against.why: The first sample (207) sat above the replicates (197-199): extra spread from rounding draws, with the mean (200.25) equal to RL's, as predicted.
The random rank-8 edit is flat at 158-167 across sizes; the rounding residue is the same kind of random edit, so it is inert.

carried.lens: sampling: temperature, top-p, entropy of the next-token distribution, what a vote over samples adds
carried.statement: A plurality vote counts only committed answers: a cap hit or a missing answer casts no vote, so a right answer facing abstentions wins outright, while one facing scattered wrong values wins only through the tie rule. A model that abstains instead of guessing (Think-SFT) votes close to pass@4. Anything that turns abstentions into finished answers (a longer cap, finishing weights) raises single samples but adds wrong votes, so the vote gains less than the singles.

holds_against.why: RL rarely abstains on fresh2026 yet gains 6.5 from the vote: with 43 % precision its right answers still coincide while the wrong ones scatter, so ties go its way less often than Think-SFT's outright wins.
The 1.5x edit abstains little and gains +14 from the vote, less than the base's +32 and Think-SFT's +32, as fewer abstentions predict.

carried.lens: sampling: temperature, top-p, entropy of the next-token distribution, what a vote over samples adds
carried.statement: Ending is a sampled event: at T 1.0 the stop token is drawn at each point where an answer could close, so lengths have a long tail that the cap cuts off. Raising the cap finishes the cut samples, right at the rate of that model's long finished answers at the same difficulty: high for Think-SFT, whose cut answers are unfinished work, low for the base and RL, whose long answers mostly guess.

holds_against.why: 23 of 93 (25 %) is well under Think-SFT's 68 % on finished answers over 12k, but the cut samples are the hardest problems; at matched difficulty its long-answer rate is about 30 %.
The base converts 4 of 64, under its 16.7 % long-answer rate, for the same reason: the cut tail is its hardest problems, where long answers are guesses.

carried.lens: when and how the model stops: token cap, loops, end-of-text, answer markers
carried.statement: RL's top singular weight directions raise the model's per-token hazard of committing to an answer and ending, in proportion to their size. In-domain directions therefore turn unfinished answers into finished ones and lengthen premature short ones. Overall right-of-finished stays roughly flat, because fixes on problems already finished offset guesses on converted cap hits. Past about 1.5x the hazard closes hard problems with guesses. The full RL delta added to Think-SFT acts the same way.

carried.lens: training data and objective: what Think-SFT imitation, RL reward and pretraining each put into the model, exposure of problems
carried.statement: Pretraining fixed, for each problem, the base's distribution over final values; the cue picks which register samples it but does not move its modal value. A vote converges to that mode, so its ceiling is the problems whose modal value is right, and samples beyond about eight only resolve ties. The plain prompt samples pretraining's terse solution register, whose accuracy falls faster with difficulty than the cued register's, so plain's share of the cued score shrinks on harder sets.

holds_against.why: Only 43 % of vote failures have agreeing wrong values; the rest are ties, which extra samples resolve, worth a few problems from 4 to 9, then a plateau at the mode.
Self-opened plain draws equal the cue, so the register is chosen at the opening of one pretrained distribution, as the mechanism says, not added by the cue.

carried.lens: weight space: the RL weight change, its top directions, scaling and transplanting it
carried.statement: RL writes its weight change in stages: the first 100 steps move weights along the reasoning-register directions that the cue's opening also drives (step-100 change about 0.03% of weight norm, activations nearly unchanged), giving the cue's gain plus a little precision; the finishing directions and the dense error-reducing remainder accumulate between steps 400 and 2,800. So a cue on an early checkpoint is redundant, and anything built from the final weights carries the late parts.

carried.lens: training data and objective: what Think-SFT imitation, RL reward and pretraining each put into the model, exposure of problems
carried.statement: RL-Zero's group-relative reward gives gradient only on prompts where some rollouts succeed and others fail, so early RL moves the policy on problems the base solves sometimes, mostly short and medium ones, and leaves problems the base rarely solves for late training. By step 100 the gain sits on MATH-500's mid-difficulty problems; on hard problems, where the cued base mostly fails or runs to the cap, step 100 plain is no better than the cued base.

holds_against.why: RL learned seen prompts that the base solves only 20.8 % of the time per sample; that rate is not zero, so group-relative gradient exists there, but it needs many steps.
Code 3.1 solves 27 % of the base's 0-of-4 problems, so those problems have a nonzero base rate and enter training late, not never.

carried.lens: when and how the model stops: token cap, loops, end-of-text, answer markers
carried.statement: As an answer grows past 12,000 tokens, the terminator the model writes is less often attached to a derived result. Base and RL end long unsolved attempts by asserting a number (66-73 % of long wrong answers); Think-SFT keeps working but drifts into Chinese past about 13,600 tokens and rarely finishes right (1 of 24). So late tokens and late finishes pay little, except for undrifted Think-SFT traces, and RL-delta hosts convert late work at RL's low long-answer precision.

holds_against.why: Think-SFT's finished answers over 12,000 tokens are right 68.2 % of the time. It keeps deriving instead of asserting; in Think-SFT the decoupling shows as script drift, which hits cut answers, not finished ones.

The base asserts as often as RL in long wrong answers (66.2 vs 72.5 %), so the effect is driven by length and shared, as stated; RL's extra assertions per sample come from finishing more long answers.

carried.lens: the grader and the measurement itself: extraction, equivalence, seeds, set composition, what a count hides
carried.statement: A count at a token cap scores every unfinished answer wrong, hiding whether it was unfinished work or a dead end. Raising the cap adds right answers in proportion to the model's share of unfinished-work cap hits: Think-SFT about one in four, RL one in ten, the base one in sixteen. Scoring the 32k text at 16,384 reproduces a 16k run, so the 32k-minus-16k difference is that yield alone.

holds_against.why: At 16k Think-SFT and RL solve equally many of the base's cap-hit MATH-500 problems: below the cap both are censored the same; the yield appears only above it.
RL's 16k count in the 32k run is 13 below its stored 206 because of a seed draw, not censoring; the paired within-run gain (+2) is the yield.

carried.lens: training data and objective: what Think-SFT imitation, RL reward and pretraining each put into the model, exposure of problems
carried.statement: On problems the base can solve, its errors are mostly per-sample slips, drawn by chance and independently at each step. Its remaining errors are misreadings and wrong plans that are set by what pretraining taught about each problem and recur across samples. Majority voting removes the slips by about 5-7 samples and then flattens at the number of problems where the base's modal answer is right, a few below pass@4, however many more samples are drawn.

carried.lens: sampling: temperature, top-p, entropy of the next-token distribution, what a vote over samples adds
carried.statement: Each sample is an independent draw: problem i is solved with a fixed probability p_i, so one cell's count varies by sqrt(sum p_i(1-p_i)), about 5-7 problems on MATH-500 and 6-9 on the 328, and same-seed reruns give new texts because vLLM is not batch-invariant. A stored single cell is one draw. New samples land around the arm's mean, not around the stored count, and a gap of a few problems between single cells is noise.

holds_against.why: An unsteered cell 3 sd above the stored 404-418 is the expected rare tail draw over dozens of cells, and its second seed fell back.
At T 0.6 loops put many problems near p = 0.5, so sum p(1-p) and the seed spread are larger there than at T 1.0.

carried.lens: the grader and the measurement itself: extraction, equivalence, seeds, set composition, what a count hides
carried.statement: Plurality votes break ties toward the lowest sample index, so at even k a 2-2 or 1-1-1-1 split is decided by sample order, not by the answers. Odd k dissolves 2-2 ties, and going from 9 to 12 samples brings them back, so the base's MATH-500 vote plateaus near 453. When abstentions become finished wrong singletons (32k cap), lone right answers end up tied and lose about half the time.

holds_against.why: On hard328 the shortest-answer tie rule moved only -1: ties there are mostly among wrong singletons, so which rule breaks them matters little; parity still sets how many ties exist.
Think-SFT's even-k vote is nearly pass@4 (244) because cap hits leave lone right answers without competing singletons; ties appear only once those answers finish.

carried.lens: training data and objective: what Think-SFT imitation, RL reward and pretraining each put into the model, exposure of problems
carried.statement: The RL update is written onto features that pretraining placed in the early and middle layers: the input directions of RL-Math's top-8 change are the ones math text drives most, and most of RL's change in model output comes from layers 0-15. Adding the directions only in the first or middle third therefore gives more of the hard-problem gain than the last third, whose main distinct job, writing the opening cue, is redundant when the cue is prefilled.

holds_against.why: One late tensor (layer 31) writes the cue and gets 397 on the plain prompt; in the layer cells the cue is prefilled, so that late-layer job adds nothing there.
Attention-only 178 against MLP-only 181 splits by module, not by depth; the depth split is untested and the KL split favours layers 0-15.

carried.lens: sampling: temperature, top-p, entropy of the next-token distribution, what a vote over samples adds
carried.statement: A weight edit shifts every next-token logit by an amount that grows with its size. Small edits move only tokens that were already uncertain (stop, hold-on, opening) and keep T 1.0 sampling coherent. Past a threshold they put mass on tokens that were near-certain, untruncated T 1.0 sampling draws them, and text decays into word strings and wrong finishes, more on long answers. The threshold follows the edit's total logit shift, so a rank-1 edit tolerates larger multiples.

holds_against.why: At a=1.5 of the full delta, 34 of 500 MATH-500 answers have word-salad tails yet score 453: the tails start after short answers are stated, so grading misses the damage.
On code the 2x edit stays at 394: code answers are short, so few tail draws accumulate before the answer is fixed.

carried.lens: when and how the model stops: token cap, loops, end-of-text, answer markers
carried.statement: A sample that hits the token cap casts no vote, so the cap acts as a free precision filter that discards long, low-precision answers. A vote gains most over one sample when many wrong answers are cut this way (cued base, Think-SFT) and least when a change makes the model finish (top-8 edit, RL delta on Think-SFT, longer cap), because finished guesses then compete with right answers. An odd number of votes removes tie losses.

carried.lens: problem structure: difficulty, domain, answer type, length of the needed derivation
carried.statement: The best size of a finishing edit depends on how many cut answers are on problems the model cannot solve. Raising the dose turns cut answers into finished ones: on solvable problems these are right, on unsolvable ones they are guesses that replace an abstention and, under a vote, outvote right samples. So the optimum dose is lower and the fall past it steeper on harder sets, while easy sets (MATH-500, code) show a flat top.

holds_against.why: Code at 2x is level with 1.5x (399): code problems have few unsolvable cut answers, so the flat top is what an easy set should show.
1.5x equals RL on MATH-500 because MATH-500 has few cap hits on unsolvable problems; the vote gap on hard328 (214 vs 221) is the guess cost.

carried.lens: Any family of causes.
carried.statement: Think-SFT's difference from the base carries long derivation; the RL-Math difference carries a controller that stops once an answer is derived. The two are orthogonal (cosine -0.00001), so their sum acts as both, but inside Think-SFT's long traces the controller is diluted and needs a = 2 to reach RL's stopping strength. At a = 2 the model derives like Think-SFT and finishes like RL on any set and seed, so gains are largest where Think-SFT caps most.

carried.lens: problem structure: difficulty, domain, answer type, length of the needed derivation
carried.statement: Each problem needs a derivation of a certain length. A cap hit is a cut answer, and raising the cap or adding finishing directions helps only where the cut text is an unfinished correct derivation (Think-SFT: about a quarter finish right). The base's and RL's cut answers are stalled, so finishing them yields guesses (base 4 of 64). So the payoff of more budget or more finishing scales with how many cut answers hold real long derivations.

holds_against.why: RL fixes the base's cap-hit problems at the matched-difficulty rate; on these sets needed length and difficulty are the same axis, so no separate stop policy is implied.
Forcing the base to commit at 8k loses problems: its long answers are stalled, not near the end of a derivation, as the mechanism says.

carried.lens: sampling: temperature, top-p, entropy of the next-token distribution, what a vote over samples adds
carried.statement: Long untruncated T 1.0 generations drift off-distribution (script switches into Chinese, restarted working) at a rate set by how far the prompt template is from the model's training format. Drifted continuations are almost never right (1 of 24 finish right). Think-SFT in its own ChatML <think> format samples a sharper, on-distribution next-token distribution, so fewer long answers drift, and its trained Answer line removes v3 undercounts; raw-template cue runs keep the drift.

carried.lens: sampling: temperature, top-p, entropy of the next-token distribution, what a vote over samples adds
carried.statement: Problems differ in solve rate far beyond binomial noise. Each arm has a block of problems it almost never samples right (base: 33 at 0 of 4 on MATH-500, against 0.5 expected) and a block where a wrong value is as likely as the right one. A vote wins only problems where the right answer is the most likely one, so it plateaus a few samples past 4, and the near-zero block caps votes on hard sets.

holds_against.why: Only 43 % of the base's vote failures are agreeing wrong groups; the rest are ties that more samples settle, worth about 5 problems by k = 9, after which the near-zero block holds.

Wang's majority curve still climbs to 93 % at 16, but it starts from 78 % under a stricter grader at T 0.6, with more problems near p = 0.5; ours starts at 89 % with the remainder in the near-zero block.

carried.lens: the grader and the measurement itself: extraction, equivalence, seeds, set composition, what a count hides
carried.statement: Under a plurality vote a cap hit or missing answer is an abstention, while a finished wrong answer is a vote against. A model's vote gain over its singles is set by how often it abstains instead of answering wrong: Think-SFT's vote nearly equals pass@4, while RL's and the edits' lose more. Raising the cap or adding finishing weight turns abstentions into mostly wrong finished answers, so singles rise while vote gains shrink.

holds_against.why: Agreeing wrong groups explain the residual base vote failures on MATH-500, where the base abstains little; abstention sets the size of the vote gain, not every failure.
The base still loses 15 problems to selection on hard328 despite 77 cap hits because its finished answers are right only ~64 % of the time; abstention lowers the loss without removing it.

carried.lens: problem structure: difficulty, domain, answer type, length of the needed derivation
carried.statement: A problem set's hardness distribution sets how much any change can move it. fresh2026 is bimodal: most problems are beyond every 7B model's reach, and a thin middle band decides every comparison. hard328 has a wider middle band. So on fresh2026, vote gains, edit gains and the gains from a longer cap all shrink toward the size of that middle band, and they compress the differences between models.

carried.lens: weight space: the RL weight change, its top directions, scaling and transplanting it
carried.statement: The RL-direction edit acts as a sum of small logit pushes, one from every layer and direction it contains, roughly proportional to each part's share of the edit. No single layer band or direction holds the finishing effect. A part of the edit acts like the whole edit scaled to that share: one third of the layers at 1.5x behaves like the whole edit at about 0.5x, and one direction like top-8 at its norm share.

holds_against.why: Layers 0-15 carry twice the KL of 16-31 at the most-different positions, but KL measures distance, not finishing; the weight change itself is flat per layer (3.0-3.2 %), and its push adds up along depth.
Removing the top 8 from RL costs only 4.6 points because RL's remaining directions also push toward finishing; that is the same additive picture.

carried.lens: weight space: the RL weight change, its top directions, scaling and transplanting it
carried.statement: The weight change of the first 100 RL steps is small (0.028 % of the weight norm) and points elsewhere than the final change (cosine 0.099). It moves the opening and register subspace and sharpens finished answers, but it does not contain the finishing directions that grow later. So step 100 writes deliberative answers with the cued base's cap-hit behaviour, adding the cue to it is redundant, and its lead over the cued base is small on every set.

holds_against.why: Step 100's finished answers are 4.6 points more often right at T 0.6; that is the small sharpening the mechanism allows, not a finishing change.
Step-100 cue 427 against plain 418 is +1.8 [-1.2, 4.8]: the cue is redundant within noise.

carried.lens: problem structure: difficulty, domain, answer type, length of the needed derivation
carried.statement: Competition problems (AIME, HMMT; most of hard328, all of fresh2026) are limited by finding a working plan, not by executing steps: the base's errors on problems it never solves are wrong plans, and RL's finished wrong answers are 67 % wrong plans. RL weights and their top directions add finishing and fewer slips but no plans, so on contest sets they track RL; only imitation of long expert traces supplies plans, visible as high precision of finished long answers.

holds_against.why: RL finishing Think-SFT's first half gains nothing over Think-SFT itself (211): the plan is already in the prefix and RL loses only on the cut prefixes, where it boxes guesses.
RL fixes the base's hard328 cap-hit problems no more than difficulty predicts, which fits plan-limited problems, not a length-specific gain.

run-05/f2-m06.statement: Weight edits merged in bf16 are realized only where an entry's change exceeds half a unit in the last place of that weight, so small edits are thresholded onto small-magnitude weights and their effective size grows faster than nominal size (a=0.25 acts like about 0.12; top-8 at nominal 1.5 acts like RL's own top-8 share). Smaller deltas such as Code-RL's lose more at 1x and peak at a larger nominal size; trained checkpoints carry no such loss.

run-02/f2-m01.statement: The autobench agent works under a fixed generation time per experiment, so it buys votes by shortening each sample (its best config: 10 samples at about 1,100 tokens each). Most MATH-500 problems are solved in under 2,000 tokens, so short samples plus a vote score well on dev100, but hard328 solutions need 6,000-14,000 tokens and short samples never reach them. For the base, each doubling of the token budget past 8,000 buys fewer problems.

run-05/f2-m01.statement: The top-8 singular directions per matrix of the RL change act as a signed termination dial spread over all layers and both module families: adding them at size s raises, monotonically in s, the chance an answer closes with a boxed result before the cap (negative s lengthens and unboxes), and modestly raises correctness on problems already finished; past 1.5x it closes unfinished hard solutions on guesses. Random rank-8 edits and Think-SFT's directions carry no dial.

run-06/f2-m03.statement: An outcome reward pays only for a gradable final answer, so its consistent gradient piles into a few singular directions that make the model complete the task in the rewarded form (boxed answer, final code block) before the cap; the rest of the update is diffuse. In-domain, the top-8 directions at 1.5x reproduce nearly all of RL's gain over the cued base. Another reward's directions give about half, random rank-8 gives nothing, and 2x commits too early.

run-05/f2-m03.statement: Each direction of an RL change acts only as far as the processed text drives its input (right) singular vectors: Math-RL's top-8 input subspaces are excited 8-11x above random by math-solution text and Code-RL's 6-9x, so an edit works in full on any problem set of its own domain and transfers to another domain in proportion to input-subspace overlap (Math with Code about 0.22-0.26, giving roughly half the in-domain effect).

round-09/stopping-m03.statement: The stop decision responds to the root of the summed squared singular values an edit adds per matrix, whatever its rank: one RL direction at 1x cut cap hits as eight at 0.5x did (51 vs 50). So top-1 at 2x and 3x act like top-8 near 1.1x and 1.6x. Above a top-subspace energy near that of the top-8 3x edit, the model degenerates into word strings that never reach an answer marker; every target edit stays below that level.

round-09/grader-m01.statement: Each posted single cell is one seeded draw: new seeds on the same weights scatter by 5-7 problems per 500 and up to 9-19 per 328, and cells picked as notable (best size, first run) sit above their model's mean. Multi-sample means regress to the pooled level of near-identical cells: step-100 plain pools with step-100 cue (same opening policy), and the 164-problem references come from draws above their own 4-sample means.

run-08/f2-m06.statement: A cap hit casts no vote: a model that runs out of tokens abstains instead of guessing, so its vote approaches pass@k (Think-SFT 241 against 244), while a model that finishes long and wrong spends votes on scattered wrong answers (RL 221 against 240). Turning abstentions into finishes (larger cap, RL directions, transplant) raises single-sample counts more than vote counts, because most converted rows are wrong and dilute the right minority.

run-08/f2-m02.statement: A count 'at 16,384' rescored from a 32k run is a different measurement from a native 16k run: rows longer than 16,384 count wrong, while a native run lets grader v3 credit a box already written inside a truncated row (RL 69 % of capped rows, base 17 %, Think-SFT rarely). So 32k-minus-16k is extension finishes only, and models that box mid-reasoning lose a few problems when rescored.

round-10/weights-m06.statement: Within the top-8 RL directions, the first singular direction of each matrix carries the format and stop part: it cuts cap hits, and at large size stops the model boxing its answer. Directions 2-8 carry the part that raises right answers on finished problems. So rank-1 edits finish without adding right answers, removing direction 1 keeps most of the correctness gain, and overdosing direction 1 produces unboxed answers that are graded wrong.

round-09/grader-m04.statement: A count's size depends on the set's difficulty mix: hard328's first 164 problems are much harder than its second half (cued base 65 vs 99), and fresh2026 is harder still. On hard items the opening (cue, step 100, self-opening) moves few problems, while answers past 16k tokens are mostly unfinished or guessed, so cap raises and votes yield less per abstention than on hard328, and plain prompts keep a falling share of the cued count.

round-09/training-m01.statement: Think-SFT imitated teacher traces inside its ChatML template, opened by <think> and closed by a final answer after the thinking block. Where and how it states the answer is learned conditional on that template. On the raw template with the cue it reasons as well but sometimes misplaces the final answer (on the line after 'Answer:'), which v3 misses. Its own template restores the trained ending: more MATH-500 answers counted, unchanged reasoning length and cap behaviour on hard328.

round-09/stopping-m04.statement: On a hard set part of every model's answers would end past 16,384 tokens, and a cut answer scores zero. A change that leaves the length distribution in place (100 RL steps, the cue on a checkpoint, a new seed or more samples) can move only the precision of finished answers. Step 100 writes cued-base lengths at T 1.0 (4,120 vs 4,008 tokens), so on hard problems it keeps the cued base's cap hits and adds a few right answers.

run-02/f2-m04.statement: A capped sample gives no answer, so in a plurality vote it abstains instead of adding a wrong value. Think-SFT's vote sits near its pass@4 because its unsolved samples run to the cap rather than box a guess. Anything that makes it finish, a 32k cap or the RL difference, turns abstentions into mostly wrong, scattered answers that tie or outvote lone right samples: single scores rise, vote gains shrink.

round-10/weights-m01.statement: The top RL-Math directions write stop and box logits additively: signed size s shifts the log-odds that an answer runs to the cap by a roughly fixed amount per unit, in either sign, on any set. Cap-hit counts therefore move with each set's base cap rate in log-odds, not by a fixed fraction. Overdose costs right answers only in proportion to a set's long unsolved answers, which it forces to finish as guesses.

round-12/s1-b.statement: Without the cue, the base at T 0.6 meets hard problems with quick, confident, finished wrong answers. These repeat across samples of the same context, so a plurality vote locks onto them. On easy MATH-500 problems the shared answer is the right one, so the vote ties the cue there. On hard328 it fixes the wrong attractor. The 4,096 cap is secondary: most of these samples finish early (mean about 1,700 tokens per sample).

run-08/f2-m05.statement: Majority vote counts answer strings: the base's wrong answers scatter (only about a quarter repeat), so the right answer is the plurality once per-sample success exceeds about 0.3, and even k leaves ties that a fixed rule breaks about half right. Vote over k therefore rises toward the number of problems whose right answer is the modal string, well below pass@k, with odd k gaining from fewer ties and returns shrinking fast after k = 4.

round-09/training-m02.statement: Think-SFT copied teacher traces produced under long budgets, and imitation carries no pressure to stop, so its 16,384-token cuts are mid-derivation work, not loops or guesses. More budget turns cut answers right at the problem's difficulty rate (about a quarter on hard328, fewer on 2026 problems). Late finishes are mostly wrong but scattered, so in a vote they seldom beat an existing right answer and add less than to single samples. RL's delta adds stopping, leaving fewer cuts to convert.

round-10/problems-m04.statement: An edit's effect splits by problem stratum: it adds right answers on mid-difficulty problems (base right in some samples), which MATH-500 and hard328 both hold in similar numbers, while cap-hit changes live only in the long-derivation tail, which MATH-500 holds about a third as densely. So point gains transfer between sets, but a MATH-500 cap-hit change equals the hard328 change times the base's MATH-500/hard328 cap-hit ratio (about 22.5/77).

round-09/stopping-m01.statement: A cut-off sample writes no answer marker, so it abstains from the plurality vote instead of voting wrong. A vote's gain over one sample therefore scales with the cap-hit share times the precision of finished answers: Think-SFT (29-46 % capped, 80-88 % precise) votes near pass@4, while RL and the 1.5x edit (5-15 % capped) gain less. A longer cap turns abstentions into mostly wrong late answers, so a vote gains far less from it than one sample does.

round-09/weights-m06.statement: Edit entries smaller than half a bf16 ulp of the weight they modify are written by stochastic rounding (written/intended cosine 0.585). The written edit is unbiased: the intended direction comes through at full nominal size, and the rounding residue is a random edit, which is inert like the random rank-8 and noise controls. Scores therefore follow the nominal dose. The residue and GPU-dependent rounding draws add sample-to-sample spread, but they do not shift the mean.

round-09/sampling-m02.statement: A plurality vote counts only committed answers: a cap hit or a missing answer casts no vote, so a right answer facing abstentions wins outright, while one facing scattered wrong values wins only through the tie rule. A model that abstains instead of guessing (Think-SFT) votes close to pass@4. Anything that turns abstentions into finished answers (a longer cap, finishing weights) raises single samples but adds wrong votes, so the vote gains less than the singles.

round-09/sampling-m05.statement: Ending is a sampled event: at T 1.0 the stop token is drawn at each point where an answer could close, so lengths have a long tail that the cap cuts off. Raising the cap finishes the cut samples, right at the rate of that model's long finished answers at the same difficulty: high for Think-SFT, whose cut answers are unfinished work, low for the base and RL, whose long answers mostly guess.

run-03/f2-m02.statement: RL's top singular weight directions raise the model's per-token hazard of committing to an answer and ending, in proportion to their size. In-domain directions therefore turn unfinished answers into finished ones and lengthen premature short ones. Overall right-of-finished stays roughly flat, because fixes on problems already finished offset guesses on converted cap hits. Past about 1.5x the hazard closes hard problems with guesses. The full RL delta added to Think-SFT acts the same way.

round-13/s4-b.statement: Any reasoning reward's top-8 directions share a generic commit-to-a-complete-answer component, whose input side is excited by code and math text alike. It sharpens the base onto its own most likely complete program, which on code is usually a passing one. The gain is limited by what the base can already write (its pass@k), not by RL-Code's level, so Math's and Code's directions add until that ceiling.

round-09/training-m04.statement: Pretraining fixed, for each problem, the base's distribution over final values; the cue picks which register samples it but does not move its modal value. A vote converges to that mode, so its ceiling is the problems whose modal value is right, and samples beyond about eight only resolve ties. The plain prompt samples pretraining's terse solution register, whose accuracy falls faster with difficulty than the cued register's, so plain's share of the cued score shrinks on harder sets.

run-05/f2-m04.statement: RL writes its weight change in stages: the first 100 steps move weights along the reasoning-register directions that the cue's opening also drives (step-100 change about 0.03% of weight norm, activations nearly unchanged), giving the cue's gain plus a little precision; the finishing directions and the dense error-reducing remainder accumulate between steps 400 and 2,800. So a cue on an early checkpoint is redundant, and anything built from the final weights carries the late parts.

round-09/training-m03.statement: RL-Zero's group-relative reward gives gradient only on prompts where some rollouts succeed and others fail, so early RL moves the policy on problems the base solves sometimes, mostly short and medium ones, and leaves problems the base rarely solves for late training. By step 100 the gain sits on MATH-500's mid-difficulty problems; on hard problems, where the cued base mostly fails or runs to the cap, step 100 plain is no better than the cued base.

round-09/stopping-m05.statement: As an answer grows past 12,000 tokens, the terminator the model writes is less often attached to a derived result. Base and RL end long unsolved attempts by asserting a number (66-73 % of long wrong answers); Think-SFT keeps working but drifts into Chinese past about 13,600 tokens and rarely finishes right (1 of 24). So late tokens and late finishes pay little, except for undrifted Think-SFT traces, and RL-delta hosts convert late work at RL's low long-answer precision.

round-09/grader-m06.statement: A count at a token cap scores every unfinished answer wrong, hiding whether it was unfinished work or a dead end. Raising the cap adds right answers in proportion to the model's share of unfinished-work cap hits: Think-SFT about one in four, RL one in ten, the base one in sixteen. Scoring the 32k text at 16,384 reproduces a 16k run, so the 32k-minus-16k difference is that yield alone.

run-06/f2-m04.statement: On problems the base can solve, its errors are mostly per-sample slips, drawn by chance and independently at each step. Its remaining errors are misreadings and wrong plans that are set by what pretraining taught about each problem and recur across samples. Majority voting removes the slips by about 5-7 samples and then flattens at the number of problems where the base's modal answer is right, a few below pass@4, however many more samples are drawn.

round-09/sampling-m01.statement: Each sample is an independent draw: problem i is solved with a fixed probability p_i, so one cell's count varies by sqrt(sum p_i(1-p_i)), about 5-7 problems on MATH-500 and 6-9 on the 328, and same-seed reruns give new texts because vLLM is not batch-invariant. A stored single cell is one draw. New samples land around the arm's mean, not around the stored count, and a gap of a few problems between single cells is noise.

round-09/grader-m05.statement: Plurality votes break ties toward the lowest sample index, so at even k a 2-2 or 1-1-1-1 split is decided by sample order, not by the answers. Odd k dissolves 2-2 ties, and going from 9 to 12 samples brings them back, so the base's MATH-500 vote plateaus near 453. When abstentions become finished wrong singletons (32k cap), lone right answers end up tied and lose about half the time.

round-09/training-m06.statement: The RL update is written onto features that pretraining placed in the early and middle layers: the input directions of RL-Math's top-8 change are the ones math text drives most, and most of RL's change in model output comes from layers 0-15. Adding the directions only in the first or middle third therefore gives more of the hard-problem gain than the last third, whose main distinct job, writing the opening cue, is redundant when the cue is prefilled.

round-09/weights-m03.statement: The part of the RL difference that sets finishing is read out late: in layers 22-31 it writes the stop and hold-on token logits ('Wait', the box, EOS) straight into the unembedding. The changes in early and middle layers alter representations that the late readout does not use for finishing. Restricted to a layer band, the late band gives most of the dial, and the early and middle bands give little over the cued base.

round-09/sampling-m04.statement: A weight edit shifts every next-token logit by an amount that grows with its size. Small edits move only tokens that were already uncertain (stop, hold-on, opening) and keep T 1.0 sampling coherent. Past a threshold they put mass on tokens that were near-certain, untruncated T 1.0 sampling draws them, and text decays into word strings and wrong finishes, more on long answers. The threshold follows the edit's total logit shift, so a rank-1 edit tolerates larger multiples.

run-03/f2-m04.statement: Graded accuracy depends on how a model ends its answer: whether the last thing written is the gradable marker (a boxed value, an Answer: line, the final python block). Under the raw template Think-SFT sometimes ends with the gold on a line v3 does not read. RL directions install one terminal marker. The native Think-SFT format ends with a post-think summary that restates the answer. Math directions push a boxed ending that competes with the final code block.

run-03/f2-m01.statement: A sample that hits the token cap casts no vote, so the cap acts as a free precision filter that discards long, low-precision answers. A vote gains most over one sample when many wrong answers are cut this way (cued base, Think-SFT) and least when a change makes the model finish (top-8 edit, RL delta on Think-SFT, longer cap), because finished guesses then compete with right answers. An odd number of votes removes tie losses.

round-09/problems-m06.statement: The best size of a finishing edit depends on how many cut answers are on problems the model cannot solve. Raising the dose turns cut answers into finished ones: on solvable problems these are right, on unsolvable ones they are guesses that replace an abstention and, under a vote, outvote right samples. So the optimum dose is lower and the fall past it steeper on harder sets, while easy sets (MATH-500, code) show a flat top.

run-02/f2-m06.statement: Think-SFT's difference from the base carries long derivation; the RL-Math difference carries a controller that stops once an answer is derived. The two are orthogonal (cosine -0.00001), so their sum acts as both, but inside Think-SFT's long traces the controller is diluted and needs a = 2 to reach RL's stopping strength. At a = 2 the model derives like Think-SFT and finishes like RL on any set and seed, so gains are largest where Think-SFT caps most.

round-09/problems-m02.statement: Each problem needs a derivation of a certain length. A cap hit is a cut answer, and raising the cap or adding finishing directions helps only where the cut text is an unfinished correct derivation (Think-SFT: about a quarter finish right). The base's and RL's cut answers are stalled, so finishing them yields guesses (base 4 of 64). So the payoff of more budget or more finishing scales with how many cut answers hold real long derivations.

run-04/f2-m05.statement: Long untruncated T 1.0 generations drift off-distribution (script switches into Chinese, restarted working) at a rate set by how far the prompt template is from the model's training format. Drifted continuations are almost never right (1 of 24 finish right). Think-SFT in its own ChatML <think> format samples a sharper, on-distribution next-token distribution, so fewer long answers drift, and its trained Answer line removes v3 undercounts; raw-template cue runs keep the drift.

round-09/sampling-m06.statement: Problems differ in solve rate far beyond binomial noise. Each arm has a block of problems it almost never samples right (base: 33 at 0 of 4 on MATH-500, against 0.5 expected) and a block where a wrong value is as likely as the right one. A vote wins only problems where the right answer is the most likely one, so it plateaus a few samples past 4, and the near-zero block caps votes on hard sets.

round-09/grader-m02.statement: Under a plurality vote a cap hit or missing answer is an abstention, while a finished wrong answer is a vote against. A model's vote gain over its singles is set by how often it abstains instead of answering wrong: Think-SFT's vote nearly equals pass@4, while RL's and the edits' lose more. Raising the cap or adding finishing weight turns abstentions into mostly wrong finished answers, so singles rise while vote gains shrink.

run-07/f2-m06.statement: A problem set's hardness distribution sets how much any change can move it. fresh2026 is bimodal: most problems are beyond every 7B model's reach, and a thin middle band decides every comparison. hard328 has a wider middle band. So on fresh2026, vote gains, edit gains and the gains from a longer cap all shrink toward the size of that middle band, and they compress the differences between models.

round-09/weights-m02.statement: The RL-direction edit acts as a sum of small logit pushes, one from every layer and direction it contains, roughly proportional to each part's share of the edit. No single layer band or direction holds the finishing effect. A part of the edit acts like the whole edit scaled to that share: one third of the layers at 1.5x behaves like the whole edit at about 0.5x, and one direction like top-8 at its norm share.

round-09/weights-m05.statement: The weight change of the first 100 RL steps is small (0.028 % of the weight norm) and points elsewhere than the final change (cosine 0.099). It moves the opening and register subspace and sharpens finished answers, but it does not contain the finishing directions that grow later. So step 100 writes deliberative answers with the cued base's cap-hit behaviour, adding the cue to it is redundant, and its lead over the cued base is small on every set.

round-09/problems-m05.statement: Competition problems (AIME, HMMT; most of hard328, all of fresh2026) are limited by finding a working plan, not by executing steps: the base's errors on problems it never solves are wrong plans, and RL's finished wrong answers are 67 % wrong plans. RL weights and their top directions add finishing and fewer slips but no plans, so on contest sets they track RL; only imitation of long expert traces supplies plans, visible as high precision of finished long answers.

round-14/s3-b.statement: At T 0.6 the plain base's long hard328 attempts fall into repetition loops that never end at any cap. Only short attempts finish, so the 12-vote counts short answers alone, and problems needing a long derivation are lost to the temperature regime, not to the 4,096 cap. The vote lifts a weak T 0.6 single sample (107/328) by about 30. A larger cap would recover almost nothing; T 1.0 would.

round-09/stopping-m02.statement: Think-SFT imitates teacher traces sized for a long budget, so on hard problems its natural stopping point lies beyond 16,384 tokens while the derivation is progressing; the cap cuts work in progress, not loops, and a longer cap recovers about a quarter of the cuts. Adding RL-delta weight moves the stopping point earlier: cap hits fall with dose (Think-SFT 94.5 to 33, base 77 to 5), and the cut work becomes finished answers at the host's long-problem precision.

run-06/f2-m05.statement: Imitation and reward write different things. Think-SFT's update, orthogonal to RL's (cosine about 0), supplies derivation quality. RL-Math's update, shaped by a reward that scores unfinished rollouts as failures, supplies pressure to finish. Added to Think-SFT, each unit of the RL change finishes more cut samples at lower precision (88 % falling toward 72 %), so right answers peak near 2x and the vote's gain shrinks to about half of Think-SFT's.

round-09/problems-m04.statement: RL fixes problems in order of the length of the derivation they need. The first 100 steps install the deliberative opening and cut per-step slips, which pays on short and medium problems (step-100 finished answers +4.6 points). Finishing long derivations under the cap is learned only after step 400. So early checkpoints sit near the cued base on long, hard problems and gain mainly on short ones, and the cue adds little to a checkpoint that already opens this way.

round-13/s1-a.statement: The kept method caps every sample at 4,096 tokens. On hard328 the cued base's right answers have a median length of about 3,900 tokens, so the cap cuts roughly half of the right-answer length mass. A cut sample casts no vote. On problems whose only right routes are long, the vote sees only short finished answers, mostly wrong on hard problems. The score is bounded by problems solvable in under 4,096 tokens, not by vote size.

round-09/training-m05.statement: The largest singular direction per matrix of RL-Math's change carries the reward's most consistent signal: write the final answer in the boxed form the verifier reads, which also ends some answers. Deciding to stop deliberating on long problems is spread over the next directions. One direction therefore cuts cap hits only partly, and scaling it mostly changes answer form, not stopping: top-1 at 2x gains little over top-1 at 1x, while eight directions together act as the finishing dial.

run-02/f2-m03.statement: The top singular directions of the RL-Math difference set when the base stops, not whether its reasoning is right: their dose sets the cap-hit rate, while right answers per finished answer stay near the base's 0.65; RL's correctness lives in the remainder of the difference. Past dose 1, extra finishes on problems the base cannot solve are guesses, so accuracy is flat from 1x to 2x, and on MATH-500, with few cap hits, the dial adds little.

run-05/f2-m02.statement: The RL change beyond its top-8 directions is a dense per-step error reducer: it lowers the base's chance of writing a slip or misreading at each step and makes right answers consistent across samples, but carries no termination drive, so alone it lengthens answers and raises cap hits. Edits holding only top-8 directions match RL per sample by finishing more, yet trail RL under voting and in domains where per-step correctness, not finishing, limits the score.

run-04/f2-m02.statement: Vote gains come in parity steps. At even k many problems end in exact ties (36 of 500 at k=4) broken by the lowest sample index, i.e. by one random draw, so an even k adds little over the odd k before it, while an odd k breaks most 2-2 and 1-1-1-1 ties with one more draw. The curve over k is therefore a zigzag rising about 1.5 problems per odd step, with flat or slightly lower even steps.

run-07/f2-m04.statement: Answer type sets what voting and grading can recover. Contest answers are integers from a wide range, so wrong answers scatter and a right answer with modest per-sample probability wins the plurality. MATH-500 answers are often expressions. There Think-SFT writes the gold on the line after 'Answer:', and v3 misses it in about 4 answers per sample. Its native template still ends on an 'Answer:' line, so that undercount stays.

run-06/f2-m02.statement: Olmo 3's pretraining and midtraining mix already contains long first-person reasoning traces, so the base holds a complete deliberative register. The cue, a self-opened draw and the first ~100 RL steps only select it. Early RL also sharpens slightly inside the register (about 2 points). So the cue adds nothing to a checkpoint that already opens itself, and it carries a fixed 55-78 % share of RL's gain across math, code and general questions.

round-13/s3-a.statement: On MATH-500 at T 1.0, the cued base's wrong answers to a problem spread over many values, while its right answers agree on one. So the plurality vote is right whenever the right answer is the mode, even below half the samples. The ceiling for votes over many samples is the number of problems where the right answer is the mode (about 470-475), not the number where it is a majority.

run-03/f2-m03.statement: Whether tokens past a cap add right answers depends on whether a model's long answers are still deriving or already guessing. Think-SFT, trained by imitation, keeps deriving until it stops, so its capped answers are unfinished work that finishes right about a quarter of the time. The base and RL close long answers with asserted numbers, so a longer cap gains them little. In its native <think> format Think-SFT thinks longer, which moves more right answers past 16,384.

round-09/problems-m01.statement: Per-problem solve probability is bimodal: each model has a block of problems it essentially never solves (base 33 of 500 at 0/4, 79 of 328 with no right sample) and a block it solves most of the time. A plurality vote only converts problems in the narrow middle band, so vote curves plateau within a few samples at the solvable fraction; a model that abstains (cap hits) instead of answering wrong has a vote close to pass@k.

round-09/stopping-m06.statement: In the terse register the base emits end-of-text almost right after its first stated result, with no check, so terse answers end within about 1,000 tokens and are wrong on any problem needing a longer derivation. A deliberative opening, self-opening, RL training or a later hold-on word lowers that post-result stop hazard. Scores of plain-prompt cells therefore depend on how many samples stay terse; on contest problems terse samples score almost nothing.

round-12/s6-b.statement: RL-Code's top-8 directions hold two separable parts. A low-dose format part (close the code block, stop before the cap) saturates by about 0.5x and fixes about 44 unformatted answers. A dose-graded correctness part raises the pass rate of programs that were already finished. It grows roughly linearly to about 1.5x and adds to the correctness part in Math's directions. About 40 of the 69 problems gained at 1x come from the correctness part.

run-04/f2-m01.statement: At T 1.0 / top-p 1.0 the cued base's wrong final answers are spread over many values (high answer-level entropy), while its right answers coincide. A plurality vote therefore picks the right value even when it is drawn in only 25-40 % of samples, and each added sample keeps resolving such problems until only near-zero-p problems remain. Long late answers (past 16k tokens) are also scattered when wrong, so finishing them adds right votes without creating wrong majorities.

round-10/stopping-m04.statement: RL's top directions shift the lm_head readout toward commit tokens (the box, end-of-text, the 'Okay' cue). The shift raises the per-token chance of ending at points where an answer is ready, and it scales with the edit's projection on that readout, not with its energy. Directions from Math, Code or IF that share the readout add up; random or Think-SFT directions add nothing. Subtracting the directions turns boxed endings into unboxed ones more than into cap hits.

run-03/f2-m06.statement: Early RL (step 100) installs the deliberative 'Okay' opening on most answers but not all. Answers that miss it fall into the base's terse register and stop before checking, and this premature stop costs accuracy. The cue removes these premature stops: a small gain at step 100, none at step 400, where the opening is near universal. So step-100 plain sits about one point above the cued base. A finishing policy arrives only in later steps.

run-06/f2-m01.statement: Think-SFT imitates teacher traces in which every stated value is derived and the answer comes only after the work, so it rarely asserts a guess: a sample cut at the cap is unfinished work, not a stall. More budget turns about a quarter of cut samples into right answers on hard sets and more on easy ones; late wrong answers scatter, so the vote keeps gaining. The habit sits in the weights, so the template changes little.

run-07/f2-m03.statement: MATH-500 errors split by problem. A slip is a per-step chance error that independent samples rarely repeat. A misreading is set up by how the problem is worded, so the same problem draws it again and again, and that wrong value keeps a stable plurality. A vote fixes slips but not misread problems, so it saturates below pass@k. Early RL steps remove slips, and later steps remove misreadings.

round-09/sampling-m03.statement: Temperature sets how often a plain prompt opens in the deliberative 'Okay' register. At T 0.6 the first tokens collapse onto the modal opening (step 100: 478 of 500); at T 1.0 a share 1-q starts elsewhere (step 100: 117 of 500; base: about 400). A prefilled cue or fixed template removes that branch, so the cue's worth at T 1.0 is (1-q) times the gap between openings, which widens on harder problems.

run-04/f2-m04.statement: A T 1.0 run is a set of independent per-problem Bernoulli draws: the run-to-run spread of a count is sqrt(sum p(1-p)), about 5-6 problems on MATH-500 and 6 on hard328 for these models, and the seed adds nothing systematic. A stored first sample is one such draw, so a 4-sample mean is 1/4 that draw plus 3/4 the model's mean, and adding one sample to a vote moves only the few problems it can flip.

run-08/f2-m04.statement: Grader v3 and the code harness score only what they extract where they look: a final 'Answer:' line or box for math, a code block for code. A template or weight edit that moves where the final answer is written changes the count without changing solving: Think-SFT on the raw template sometimes puts it on the line after 'Answer:' (about 4 lost per 500); Math-RL directions carry a boxed ending a code extractor misses.

run-07/f2-m05.statement: Too large a finishing dose makes the model stop before its derivation is complete. The cost grows with how long a derivation the problem needs: on hard328's long problems a 2x edit commits early and right answers fall, while short problems finish well within the shortened span. Over-dosing therefore costs little on MATH-500 and on short code tasks. The cost of a cut answer, by contrast, belongs to the opposite end of the length range.

round-09/weights-m04.statement: Moved onto another model that shares the base, the RL-Math difference acts as a finishing operator on that model's own trajectories. It does not add correctness. On Think-SFT it closes long, unfinished but sound work earlier, so cap hits fall and right-of-finished drops toward RL's level. The gain is limited by how much of the recipient's cut work was sound. Prompt or template changes on Think-SFT alone (no delta) leave its finishing rate and precision unchanged.

round-13/s4-a.statement: RL-Code's code gain sits almost entirely in its own top-8 directions, and in early/middle layers it raises the pass rate of finished programs, not just how often a program finishes. At 1.5x it matches RL-Code. Math's directions help code only through the shared finishing channel (fewer cap hits and missing code blocks), passing those recovered answers at the base rate. With Code's directions already finishing nearly everything, adding Math's gives little.

round-10/weights-m05.statement: Math-RL and Code-RL directions share part of their input subspace (overlap 0.22-0.26, random 0.002), and that part writes a reward-general readout: the deliberative opening, hold-on words and finishing. The rest of each change is domain-specific and nearly orthogonal (whole-change cosine under 0.03). Stacking the two edits counts the shared readout twice, which overdoses finishing, and adds each domain remainder once, so math gets Code's remainder only where it overlaps.

run-07/f2-m01.statement: Each problem needs a derivation of a given length; past the 16,384 cap the answer is cut and scores zero. Extra budget or a finishing weight edit only converts cut answers into finished ones, and a converted answer is right at the rate the model reaches on problems that long and hard: about 25-30 % on hard328, about 45 % on MATH-500's long tail, under 20 % on fresh2026 contest problems. Finished short answers are untouched.

run-06/f2-m06.statement: No model's score depends on having seen the test problems. RL's training prompts were filtered to problems the base fails, Think-SFT's data matches the test sets in only a handful of prompts, and every gain holds on 2026 problems. So each arm's share of the base-to-RL gap belongs to its weights, not to the set: shares measured on hard328 carry over to fresh2026 once rescaled to the base and RL levels there.

run-04/f2-m03.statement: Under T 1.0 stopping is a sampled event: at each position the model draws a commit/stop token with a small hazard, so the cap-hit share is a survival probability. RL's top-8 directions add a near-constant logit to that hazard (cap hits 96, 77, 46, 25, 5 along the dial); dose multiplies it. Where the base fails by not stopping (short code tasks, fresh contests) the dial converts unfinished samples, at precision below the base's finished answers.

run-07/f2-m02.statement: An RL run's top weight directions write a habit for its own domain's answers. For Math-RL that habit is to deliberate, check, and finish with one boxed answer; for Code-RL it is to reason, then finish with one final python block that passes the tests. In its own domain the top-8 edit carries about two thirds of RL's gain at 1x and nearly all of it at 1.5x. On another domain it carries about half as much.

round-10/weights-m03.statement: The effect of an added RL change depends on the host. Think-SFT's high-rank imitation change (3.7 % of weight norm, top 8 directions hold 2 %) already sets the long-reasoning features that RL's directions read, so RL's push has about a quarter of its effect on the base: a=1 cut Think-SFT's cap hits by 20 %, not 74 %. The response is weak but stable, no breakdown up to 4x. Its correctness covers every domain in its traces.

round-09/weights-m01.statement: The commit-and-stop readout sits mainly in the top singular direction of each matrix of the RL-Math difference. The size of that one direction (its singular value times the scale) sets how often the model finishes. Breakdown into word strings also depends on that per-direction size, not on how many directions are added: about 2x over-commits on long problems, and about 3x on the top direction breaks generation, whether 1 direction or 8 are scaled.

run-02/f2-m05.statement: The RL-Math difference carries RL's habit of ending a long unsolved attempt with an asserted, underived number (per 1,312 hard328 samples RL finishes long and wrong 381 times, the base 281). Added to another model it turns unfinished attempts into such guesses and cuts slower derivations short. On new problems, where RL's finished precision is 43 %, the guesses are wrong, so gains measured on hard328 shrink or reverse; on MATH-500 it is neutral.

run-08/f2-m01.statement: Each one-sample count is one seed's draw: the model branches at forks with fixed per-problem probabilities, so a cell has a sampling SD of about 5-6 problems on MATH-500, 7-9 on hard328 and 3 on fresh2026, plus small runner drift. A stored sample 0 is an unselected draw, so a 4-sample mean is that value shrunk slightly toward the cell's structural prior (neighbouring checkpoints, cue effect).

round-11/s2-b.statement: An RL run's task-specific policy lies almost entirely in the top-8 directions per matrix of that run's own delta, read through the inputs of its own task. So 1.5x of RL-Code's directions is a copy of RL-Code, and RL deltas for different tasks occupy nearly orthogonal subspaces that add without interference. Other rewards' directions transfer only a shared finishing part (cap hits, missing answer blocks), not task skill.

round-10/problems-m03.statement: A code problem needs a short single-function artifact judged by hidden tests. The base's code deficit is mostly answers with no closed code block or cut off, not wrong logic, so any model or edit that writes a closed block recovers most of the gap; the ceiling is set by under-specified MBPP+ tests (about 405 of 538), which RL-Code (401) already nears. On math the matching lever is a terminal answer statement, which the plain base lacks.

round-10/grader-m06.statement: Each set holds items no model can be credited on: defective or unparseable golds, LLM-transcribed 2026 statements, and problems no arm ever solves (6 of MATH-500, about 80-90 of hard328). The count's ceiling is the set size minus these, so vote and long-cap gains compress as a model nears it: Think-SFT's vote already sits at pass@4, and extra samples or tokens add only on reachable unsolved items, never on the floor.

round-10/problems-m05.statement: Each set has problems that no reweighting of a host's own solution paths reaches (hard328: about 79 the base never solves even after restarts; MATH-500: about 15). Weight edits and their combinations only reweight paths the host already has, so scores saturate below that host's reach: stacking finishing directions adds little once most reachable problems finish, and votes stop near pass@k. Only a host with more reach (Think-SFT) raises the ceiling.

round-09/grader-m03.statement: An edited model is not seed-paired with the stored base: BF16 rounding of any edit changes every text, so a functionless edit lands at the edit null (random rank-8 cells 158-167, mean about 161 on hard328 with the cue), not at the base's 164 draw. A partial edit's count is that null plus its share of the replicated full-edit gain (200.25, not the selected 203); halves of the edit add up to the whole.

round-13/s6-b.statement: HumanEval+/MBPP+ are easy for the cued base: most problems it fails in one sample it passes in others, so the code gap is almost all per-sample reliability. Code-RL's top-8 directions lower the per-step error rate on reasoning text everywhere, as Math's dial does on finished-wrong math (result-124593). On a set whose gap is reliability, that recovers nearly all of RL's gain. On hard328, where a third of the gap needs answers the base never writes, it recovers less.

run-05/f2-m05.statement: Imitation (Think-SFT) and RL weight changes are orthogonal (cosine -0.00001) and read different input subspaces, so their effects superpose: Think-SFT supplies high precision on finished answers but no termination drive and runs long; adding a(RL - base) adds RL's finishing push without disturbing SFT's precision, costing only on newly finished hard problems. Prompt format changes how the SFT part is engaged, not finishing, so Think-SFT's cap hits follow the token budget.

round-10/problems-m06.statement: An RL run's finishing habit is calibrated to the derivation lengths of its training domain. Code-RL learned to close at code-answer lengths (about 4k tokens), so its directions make math answers stop earlier: harmless on short MATH-500 problems, costly on long hard328 derivations (178 vs Math's 192, at fewer tokens). Math directions, calibrated to long derivations, have no room to act on short code tasks and give a partial gain there. Mixed edits inherit the shorter calibration on long problems.

run-04/f2-m06.statement: Adding RL-direction weight to a model concentrates its answer-level distribution: samples of one problem agree more, right or wrong. Higher dose therefore raises single-sample accuracy where answers are short but shrinks what a vote adds (vote/single 1.21 base, 1.07 for the 1.5x edit, 1.09 for Think-SFT + 2x on fresh2026). On short exact outputs such as code, concentration has no truncation cost, so code accuracy does not fall back at 2x as math did.

round-10/training-m05.statement: Think-SFT's teacher traces cover competition problems (olympiad-style math and contest code) far more densely than the 3.1 RL prompts, which were filtered to problems the base fails. Imitation transfers whole solution routines for those problem types, not copies of items, so Think-SFT's lead over RL grows with competition difficulty (hard328, 2026 contests) and vanishes on MATH-500; adding the RL difference to it supplies closing, not routines.

round-09/problems-m03.statement: Easy problems need short derivations, and on them a model answers in a short register. At T 1.0 the plain prompt's terse register derails on these short problems (plain base loses 28 points on short quartiles, none on the longest), while the deliberative register survives. Edits or prompts that install deliberation lengthen short answers on easy problems; the leftover short answers are mostly right, and the residual quick wrong answers sit on problems the cued base usually solves.

round-10/stopping-m03.statement: Think-SFT was trained to end its reasoning at a </think> boundary and then write one short final answer and end-of-text. The raw template with the base's cue gives it no boundary, so after solving it keeps writing (re-checks, extra code blocks, new attempts) and stops late. In its own ChatML format it closes at the boundary: fewer answers reach 16k and output after the answer stops, with the same precision on finished answers.

run-02/f2-m02.statement: The cued base's wrong answers on a problem rarely share a value: slips are per-sample chance events that land on scattered numbers, while right answers coincide. A plurality vote therefore wins a problem once the right share exceeds the largest wrong-value share, far below one half, and keeps converting such problems as samples are added, with no plateau by 12. The loss is in ties, which odd sample counts and more samples dissolve.

round-11/s6-b.statement: Overdose costs accuracy only where the edit pushes a quantity that trades against correctness past its RL optimum. Math directions carry a math-specific stop-checking push whose optimum is near 1.5x on any math set, short or long; beyond it, checking that would catch errors is skipped. Code directions push code-block format and termination, which saturate (no-code and cap hits reach 0) and do not trade against a program's correctness, because tests, not self-checks, decide passing. So code plateaus at 2x.

run-03/f2-m05.statement: A trace can degenerate before it ends, into word strings, a switch to Chinese script or repeated windows, and a degenerate trace almost never ends right. The hazard of this grows with edit size (word strings at 2-3x) and with tokens already generated (median first script switch near token 13,600). So oversized edits, and the late part of very long Think-SFT traces, lose answers. A smaller edit or a shorter trace keeps them. At T 1.0 classic loops are absent.

round-11/s4-b.statement: Besides finishing, the top RL directions sharpen the base toward its own most likely correct solution on problems it already solves in some samples. HumanEval+ and MBPP+ consist almost entirely of such problems (high base pass@k), so at 1x most of the code gap closes through reliability on finished answers, not through cap hits. Gains from Math and Code directions add on code, and the effect needs base capability rather than a short answer length.

run-08/f2-m03.statement: The RL-direction edits add to a count mostly by converting cap hits into finished answers; the count hides the split: gain = cap hits removed x right rate on converted rows + a smaller rise in finished precision. hard328 gives the dial 77 cap hits to convert; short HumanEval+/MBPP+ answers rarely reach the cap, so the same edits move few problems there, and past 1.5x only the precision loss remains.
